name: Hand-formed plant-fibre paper
summary: Sheets formed from plant fibres suspended in water made a light, flexible writing surface; Han-period fragments from Gansu are among the earliest written examples.
description: A flexible, nonwoven sheet made by dispersing plant fibres in a water suspension and forming them together into a coherent surface that can carry writing. The node covers a process class, with distinct witnesses whose fibre mixtures, moulds and quality varied. It is structurally different from a sheet of layered strips of papyrus pith.
tier_reason: Paper as a reproducible writing/printing substrate supports administration, mathematical transmission and printing across regions and generations.

impact.note: The scoring guide's reach 3 example, a new cheap writing surface on which printing, record-keeping and many later fields stood.

why: Han writers relied on heavy bamboo and wooden slips or costly silk, so a cheap, light writing surface met a real need.

date.label: By approximately 9 CE
date.basis: Yi and Lu assign the written fragments to Western Han; 9 CE is the Metropolitan Museum’s period endpoint and is a contextual interpretive bound, not a direct sample date.

events.statement: Yi and Lu report two written Xuanquanzhi fragments as Western Han paper; Pan also identifies written Xuanquan paper as hemp, while separate site studies describe formed fibre sheets and ink writing.
events.scope: Written fragments from the Han post-site described by Pan as hemp paper; individual written fragments are not explicitly matched here to a particular microscopy specimen.
applications: Written information on a flexible fibre sheet
events.population: People who wrote on the Xuanquanzhi fragments or used them at the post site
events.caveats: The particular writer and date are not known. The Western Han assignment and paper identity follow published, contested interpretations including Pan’s identification of the written material as hemp; the writing fragments are not individually matched here to the separate fibre-study sample. Other early finds, including Fangmatan and Baqiao, have disputed dates or material identifications. The Met’s October 2000 chronology gives an approximately 109 CE earliest surviving written hemp-paper claim rather than the earlier Xuanquan attribution, without directly examining those specimens in its account. The latest bound is the contextual end of the Western Han, not a demonstrated first use, invention or universal availability.

evidence.supports: The Met chronology gives a later approximately 109 CE earliest written hemp-paper claim, without discussing the Xuanquan identification.
Pan identifies Xuanquan paper bearing characters as hemp and gives a Western Han date estimate; he reports separate material examination.
The author reports fibres and inferred mould-forming in a sample of Xuanquanzhi ancient papers, with ink on some pieces.

evidence.locator: Named article abstract in institutional issue listing
evidence.supports: The authors assign two archaeological layers to the Western Han and interpret the relevant fibre sheets as made with a pouring method.
Yi and Lu report two Xuanquanzhi paper fragments bearing writing of Western Han date; paleography is their basis for narrower suggested periods.
Metropolitan Museum chronology places the end of the Western Han period in 9 CE; this is a contextual upper bound, not the dated act of writing.

date.label: By approximately 220 CE
date.basis: Wang and Li classify the sample as Eastern Han; the final year 220 is an approximate contextual upper bound, not a directly measured date.

events.statement: A later written Hantanpo fragment was reported as a cohesive, well-mixed plant-fibre sheet.
events.scope: Written Eastern Han fibre-sheet fragment examined by Wang and Li.
applications: Written information on a cohesive fibre sheet
events.population: The unidentified writer and users of the Hantanpo fragment
events.caveats: The earlier study calls Hantanpo the earliest known written paper in its 1980 state of evidence; it did not examine the subsequently excavated Xuanquanzhi fragments. The date is a period bound, not direct sample dating or evidence for a connection between the two sites.

evidence.locator: AATA abstract, Eastern Han Hantanbo specimen
evidence.supports: Reports the fragment’s writing and cohesive well-mixed fibres and infers hand sheet-forming; the study predates the Xuanquanzhi excavations.
The Metropolitan Museum chronology places the end of the Eastern Han in 220 CE.
